native_result.query: How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?
native_result.HypoA: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: Age is negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in (DISSAVED). In the NLSY79 1989 cross-section (n=12,686, ages 24-32, base rate 23.6%), the main model DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE_2 + INCOME + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC (linear probability model, HC1-robust) gives -0.0076 per year of age, i.e. about 0.8 percentage points lower probability of dissaving per additional year (SE 0.0016, p ~ 1e-5), with a negative quadratic term AGE_2 (-0.145 pp per year^2, p = 0.059) so the decline steepens with age. The relation is approximately monotone decreasing and essentially linear inside the observed 24-32 window: predicted probability falls from 25.1% at age 24 to 18.7% at age 32, a drop of -6.4 percentage points (95% CI -9.0 to -3.9; logit -6.3 pp; flexible age dummies -7.2 pp; raw gap -7.3 pp), roughly a 26% relative reduction. Flexible age dummies show no significant departure from age 24 up to age 29 but significantly lower dissaving at 30-32 (-4.0 to -7.2 pp), and they do not improve on a single linear age term (LR = 11.1 on 7 df, p = 0.13), so no U-shaped or inverted-U pattern is supported. Robust to adding BMI, to using log income, and to logit/probit instead of the LPM. A three-state check (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) shows that with age the 'savings increased' share rises from 30% to 55% while 'unchanged' falls from 44% to 26% and 'dissaved' falls from 25% to 19%, confirming a real shift toward positive saving rather than an artefact of the dichotomy. Interpretation, not a demonstrated finding: this is consistent with age differences in time preference (younger adults discount the future more and draw down savings more often). Because it is a single cross-section in 1989, the estimate mixes age, cohort and period effects and should not be read as the causal effect of ageing; income is partly imputed (31% of rows share one value, plus top-coded values) and no survey weights are available, so magnitudes are sample-specific.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 x 9, no missing, AGE_2 = AGE^2, DISSAVED and SAMESAVE mutually exclusive, overall P(DISSAVED)=0.2355). 2) Descriptives by age year (rates of dissaving / unchanged / saved more, income medians). 3) Hierarchical LPM (HC1) and logit (HC1) models: raw age+age^2; M1 = age+age^2+INCOME+GENDER+BLACK+HISPANIC (main); M2 = M1+BMI; M1 with log income. SAMESAVE deliberately excluded as a regressor. 4) Functional form: LPM with age dummies 25-32 (ref 24) plus M1 controls, joint F test, LR test of dummies vs a single linear age term, AGE^2 Wald test, block contrast 30-32 vs 24-29. 5) Average predicted probabilities at each age with delta-method SEs (LPM, logit, probit) and marginal effect of +1 year of age. 6) Contrast 32 vs 24 in percentage points with 95% CIs across all estimators. 7) Three-state multinomial logit (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) as an interpretation check. 8) Figure: observed rates with 95% CIs plus fitted M1 and crude age-only curves (SVG, generated without matplotlib). All steps in analysis/nls_dissave_age_analysis.py, executed end to end (exit 0); outputs in analysis/results_log.txt and the CSV tables.

sub_hypo.context: Respondents in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY79), with age measured in 1989.
sub_hypo.relations: AGE has a negative coefficient (-0.0422) in a logistic regression predicting DISSAVED: younger respondents are more likely to withdraw more from savings than they deposit, controlling for income, BMI, race indicators (BLACK and HISPANIC), and gender indicators (MALE and FEMALE).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).

sub_hypo.text: Age is negatively associated with the likelihood of dissaving, with an approximately monotone decreasing, essentially linear relationship over ages 24–32.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1989 cross-section: 12,686 respondents aged 24–32, with an overall dissaving rate of 23.6%. Estimates are sample-specific and noncausal: age, cohort and period effects are mixed, income is partly imputed and top-coded, and survey weights are unavailable.
sub_hypo.relations: Controlling for income, gender, Black and Hispanic indicators, the HC1-robust linear probability model estimates about 0.8 percentage points lower dissaving probability per additional year (−0.0076; SE 0.0016; p approximately 1e-5). The negative quadratic term (−0.145 percentage points per year squared; p = 0.059) suggests a steepening decline, but no U-shaped or inverted-U pattern is supported. Predicted dissaving falls from 25.1% at age 24 to 18.7% at age 32: −6.4 percentage points (95% CI −9.0 to −3.9), approximately a 26% relative reduction.

sub_hypo.text: Flexible age estimates show significantly lower dissaving at ages 30–32 than at age 24, but no significant differences through age 29 and no significant improvement over a linear age specification.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1989 cross-section, ages 24–32; age-dummy models use age 24 as the reference and adjust for the main-model controls.
sub_hypo.relations: Ages 25–29 do not differ significantly from age 24; ages 30–32 have significantly lower dissaving probabilities by 4.0–7.2 percentage points. Age dummies do not significantly improve on a single linear age term (LR = 11.1, 7 df, p = 0.13).

sub_hypo.text: The negative age–dissaving association is robust to adjustment for BMI, use of log income, and alternative probability models.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1989 cross-section of 12,686 respondents aged 24–32; robustness checks extend or modify the main adjusted model.
sub_hypo.relations: The negative association persists when BMI is added, income is log-transformed, or logit/probit replaces the linear probability model. The age-32 versus age-24 contrast is −6.3 percentage points under logit and −7.2 percentage points with flexible age dummies, compared with a raw gap of −7.3 percentage points.

sub_hypo.text: Increasing age is associated with a shift toward positive saving, rather than merely a change induced by dichotomizing saving behavior.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 1989 cross-section, ages 24–32; a three-state saving analysis distinguishes saved more, unchanged savings, and dissaved. SAMESAVE is not a regressor in the main dissaving models.
sub_hypo.relations: Across the observed age range, the share whose savings increased rises from 30% to 55%, the unchanged share falls from 44% to 26%, and the dissaved share falls from 25% to 19%. Saved more is the remaining state when both DISSAVED and SAMESAVE are zero.
